extracted.intended_audience: readers of moral philosophy, theology, and general readers of Pascal's Pensees
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short numbered aphorisms and meditations about human character, passions, diversion, vanity, misery, and the necessity of seeking God; useful as prompts or themes in moral/theological reflection. The text comprises concise observations rather than procedural instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness of falsity of present pleasures (110)
rubrics_metrics.description: The awareness that present pleasures are false, combined with ignorance of the vanity of absent pleasures, produces inconstancy in people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the psychological source of changeable desires: we know present pleasures are not wholly true but fail to see that future pleasures are equally vain. No scoring guidance; example framing is general psychological observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconstancy (111–114, 127)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human inconstancy: people are variable and changeable; one must learn how to 'play' upon human dispositions (analogy of organs with misarranged pipes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes metaphors (organs/keys) and examples (we weep and laugh at the same thing; Sultan combining opposites). Implicit advice: to deal with people one must know their proper 'keys' (i.e., dispositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety (114–116)
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything exhibits infinite variety — voices, gestures, vines, parts of man; one cannot judge the same thing in the same way continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises artistic distance ('stand at a distance, but not too far') and accepts irreducible multiplicity in theology and human composition (dissection yields many ‘sciences’).

rubrics_metrics.name: All is one, all is different (116)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man contains multiple 'natures' and vocations; unity and difference coexist within the human person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions how each person chooses their vocation — often by imitation of what is praised. Encourages awareness of internal plurality when assessing human behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small features shape inclinations (The heel of a slipper) (117)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial or minute observable features (a well-turned heel, small habits) often determine our inclinations and judgments of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attention to small cues when explaining social preferences and choices; these minor details produce large social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief talent rules the rest (118)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal talent in a person tends to dominate and direct other faculties or inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a person, consider the dominant talent as primary explanatory factor for behavior and choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature imitates herself; principles and consequences (119–121)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural processes repeat and mirror themselves (seed-ground-fruit analogy); finite things multiply to give the appearance of infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy used to reason about causation, order, and the relationship between principles and consequences; suggests looking for recurrent structural patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time heals griefs and quarrels (122)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change over time makes former offenses and passions fade; people encountered after generations are not the same persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporal distance as explanatory factor for reconciliation and changing affections (example: lovers of ten years earlier are different people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different viewpoints produce different judgments (124)
rubrics_metrics.description: We view things not only from different sides but 'with different eyes' and are unwilling to see them as identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting actions or works, account for perspective shifts and the desire not to find sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraries in man (125)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is full of contradictions — naturally credulous and incredulous, timid and rash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accommodate opposing tendencies when describing or evaluating human conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of man: dependency and desire of independence (126)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human condition mixes dependency, desire for independence, and need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining motives, balance these conflicting drives as coexisting facts, not mutually exclusive states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of man: inconstancy, weariness, unrest (127–131)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans are restless and weary; inability to remain at rest produces misery — complete rest equals death metaphorically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: to cure complaints about hardship, give an idle laborer nothing to do (illustrative point about restlessness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Struggle pleases, not victory (135)
rubrics_metrics.description: People enjoy seeing conflict and the struggle of opposites rather than the achieved victory; the search itself pleases more than possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tastes in spectacle and intellectual dispute: conflict provides emotion, final resolution tends to satiation; applies to play, truth-seeking, drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: A trifle consoles and a trifle distresses (136)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small things can have disproportionate emotional effects, either consoling or distressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing human response, account for the outsized power of trivial incidents to alter mood or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversion: inability to stay quietly at home as root of unhappiness (139)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of human unhappiness stems from man's inability to remain quietly in his room; people pursue bustle (court, war, play) to escape self-reflection on mortality and misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive examples: hunting, play, office, company; author argues diversion functions to avert thought of death and the human condition. Anti-pattern: advising someone to 'live quietly' misunderstands human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chase versus quarry — pursuit desired, not the object (displacement of ends) (139–140)
rubrics_metrics.description: People seek the excitement of pursuit (the chase) rather than the object itself (the quarry); the activity that distracts is the sought end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains gambling, conquest, study: people prefer the thrill of the endeavor and the imagined gain (which they'd reject as a mere gift) to the calm possession. Practical implication: creating artificial challenges fuels engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversion as a means to avoid thinking of death (169–171, 166)
rubrics_metrics.description: People use diversion to prevent thought of death, misery, and ultimate questions; diversion comforts but masks the root problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues this avoidance is central to human behavior; paradoxically, diversion both consoles and perpetuates misery by preventing self-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kings require constant diversion (142–143)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even kings, despite grandeur, require diversions to prevent self-reflection and consequent misery; attendants ensure no blank in their leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example-driven claim: high office supplies continuous distractions precisely because solitude would make rulers miserable; not a moral judgment about kings as Christians but as kings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversion is dangerous because it hinders reflection and ruins us (171)
rubrics_metrics.description: While diversion consoles us for miseries, it is our greatest misery because it chiefly stops us from reflecting and finding a permanent remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative warning: diversion is double-edged — immediate relief but long-term spiritual/ethical cost; encourages deeper reflection rather than perpetual distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: One thought at a time (145)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans cannot think of two things simultaneously — attention is unitary, which shapes how we are 'lucky' in worldly matters but not before God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for persuasion and instruction: capture attention with a single focus rather than scattering it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man is made to think; the world prefers diversion (146)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity and duty of man is to think (beginning with self, its author and end), but the world's occupations (games, power, arts) avoid these thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for prioritizing inner reflection and philosophical/theological inquiry over mere worldly pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity and living an imagined life (147–150)
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer to live an imaginary life in the minds of others, cultivating reputation, and often separate virtues from the self to attach them to that imaginary persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes the paradox of renouncing authentic qualities to secure reputation; warns readers about the triviality of fame and the social mechanics of vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory and admiration spoil from infancy (151)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration and praise from infancy induce vanity; absence of such stimulus can lead to carelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational implication: praise shapes character and can create dependence on external validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride and curiosity as forms of vanity (152–153)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity often masks vanity — many seek knowledge primarily to speak of it; pride drives actions even amid suffering if they confer reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical lens on motives for learning and experiences (e.g., travel for stories), recommending self-examination of motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value (and danger) of friendship and choice of friends (155)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true friend is a great advantage for reputation and support, but one must choose friends well, since fools will not sustain one's honour in adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: friendships are useful for social backing, but evaluate friends' influence and loyalty before relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding to pain vs pleasure — mastery and shame (160)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yielding to pain is viewed as honorable because one wills it to conquer oneself; yielding to pleasure is shameful because pleasure attracts and masters us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral distinction: deliberate self-denial confers mastery and glory, whereas surrender to pleasure shows slavery to desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble deeds are most estimable when hidden (159)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done to remain hidden are most noble; publicity spoils the moral worth of good deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative preference for humility and secrecy in virtue; caution that minimal publication can corrupt the best motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present, past, future — we seldom live in the present (172)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans occupy themselves with past or future; the present is used as a means, not an end, so we never truly live but only hope to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological diagnosis of chronic dissatisfaction; implicit counsel to reorient towards present-mindedness to counter perpetual postponement of happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misery and human ignorance of self (171, 174–176)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human misery is profound; figures like Solomon and Job best spoke of it. People often misjudge their own health or state (examples: unaware of approaching death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical and anecdotal illustration (Cromwell, medical ignorance) to show how small causes can upend great designs; moral: reflect on fragility rather than presume security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratagem for addressing unbelief and promoting religion (Section III, 184–187)
rubrics_metrics.description: To incite search after God, one should show religion is not contrary to reason, make it venerable (to inspire respect), lovable (to make good men hope it is true), and finally prove it true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic order for apologetics: begin by reconciling faith and reason, cultivate respect, make the faith attractive morally, then argue for its truth; avoid forcing belief by terror (terorrem potius quam religionem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward unbelievers: pity, not scorn; learn what you attack (188–194)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach unbelievers with pity; they are wretched. Do not revile them needlessly. Those who attack religion should at least understand the religion they criticize — negligence in inquiry is inexcusable when one's eternity is at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel for dialogue: begin with compassion, avoid gratuitous reproach, insist that critics honestly search and examine religious claims before dismissing them. Practical admonition: distinguish sincere seekers from the merely negligent or boastful.
